scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: packet forwarding disabled (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward)

agent.diagnosis_text:
- Affected component: Linux netfilter firewall on router1 (iptables FORWARD chain).
- Mechanism: Transit traffic between interfaces must traverse the FORWARD chain. On router1, kernel IP forwarding is enabled (net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1) and routing/RIP are correct, but an iptables rule unconditionally drops all forwarded packets. This blocks any inter-VLAN/segment traffic transiting router1 while still allowing local pings to router1 itself (INPUT/OUTPUT chains), which matches users being able to ping their gateway but not reach remote networks.
- Localization: router1; the FORWARD chain contains a blanket drop: “-A FORWARD -j DROP”. Counters confirm it is actively dropping packets (18 packets, 1512 bytes). Routing tables in FRR show valid RIP routes to 1.0.0.0/8 (Server Room) and 128.168.0.0/16 (Internet Lab), so the control plane is fine; the data plane is being filtered.
- Root cause: Misconfigured firewall on router1 placing a catch‑all DROP in the FORWARD chain, breaking inter-network forwarding.
- Corrective fix: Remove or override the drop rule so transit is permitted. For immediate relief: iptables -D FORWARD 1 (if it’s the only rule) or iptables -F FORWARD, and ensure policy is ACCEPT: iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT. Then persist the change via your iptables-save mechanism or configure explicit ACCEPT rules between required subnets before any DROP. Afterward, verify by pinging from 192.168.3.0/24 to 1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 and ensure FORWARD counters no longer climb for DROPs.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly localizes the fault to router1 (multiple mentions stating the FORWARD chain on router1 is dropping transit packets).
